vignette:
He is seventy-one now, a married man from Oceania who still works as a cashier at a neighborhood shop, mostly because he likes the routine and says sitting at home too long makes his mind “wander to the wrong places.” When he first speaks about what happened, he does so carefully, as if he is handling something sharp. The memory begins several years earlier, on an ordinary late afternoon after work. He is walking toward the bus stop when a violent incident unfolds just ahead of him. He sees another man attacked suddenly and brutally in the street. For a few seconds he does not understand what he is looking at. Then there is shouting, people scattering, the sound of something hitting the pavement, and the sight of the injured man’s body lying in a way that does not seem possible. He remembers freezing. He wants to move forward and backward at the same time. He feels ashamed afterward that he cannot make his legs work. By the time others rush in, call for help, and the attacker is gone, he is trembling so hard he cannot hold his phone.

That night he does not sleep. Each time he closes his eyes he sees the man on the ground, the suddenness of it, the helplessness on bystanders’ faces, his own useless stillness. He lies beside his wife staring into the dark, listening for sounds outside the house. In the days that follow, he tells himself he is lucky he was not physically harmed, that he should simply be grateful and move on. Instead, small details from the scene begin attaching themselves to everyday life. The sound of raised voices on the street makes his chest clench. If someone drops a box behind him at work, his whole body jolts before he can stop it. He starts scanning faces without meaning to, watching hands, exits, and doorways.

Before the incident, he likes talking with customers. He knows many of them by name, jokes with schoolchildren buying snacks, and asks older regulars about their families. Afterward, standing behind the register feels exposed. He becomes acutely aware that he is trapped in one place while everyone else moves around him. When young men enter the shop arguing loudly or moving quickly, he feels heat rise up his neck and his palms become wet. He keeps his eyes on the till, pretending to count change while listening for any sign that something is about to happen. Sometimes he loses track of the numbers on the screen because in his mind he is back on that street, seeing the man fall. A customer asks him to repeat the total and he realizes he has not heard a word they said.

His wife notices the changes before he admits them. He is more irritable, snapping at small things and then going quiet. He begins avoiding the route where the assault occurred, even though it is the shortest way to work. If a television program shows violence, he leaves the room immediately. Family members invite him to community gatherings, but he often says he is too tired. The truth is that crowded places make him uneasy. He sits only if he can face the entrance. He studies strangers for signs of danger and cannot relax enough to enjoy himself. He feels guilty for this, especially when his grandchildren want him to come watch them perform or play. He goes sometimes, but spends the entire event tense, unable to follow what is happening in front of him because he is busy monitoring everyone around him.

Sleep remains one of the hardest parts. He wakes drenched in sweat after dreams that are not exact replays but carry the same terror and helplessness. On some nights he hears the shouting again just as he is drifting off, vivid enough that he sits up in bed with his heart pounding. In the morning he is exhausted and ashamed that one moment he witnessed has come to dominate so much of his life. He tells himself he is an old man now, that he should be stronger, that other people have survived worse. Yet the self-criticism only deepens his sense of isolation.

What troubles him most is how the world no longer feels ordinary. He used to think of danger as something distant, something that happened elsewhere or to other people. Now he experiences it as close, random, and always about to break through the surface of daily life. Even while scanning groceries and handing over receipts, part of him remains braced for catastrophe. He still goes to work, still comes home to his wife, still keeps his routines, but everything takes more effort. He says he misses the version of himself who could stand in a line, walk down a street, or hear a sudden noise without feeling his body prepare for disaster.
